title: Matthew 8:23–27
context: Jesus embarks; a sudden storm terrifies the disciples while He sleeps. Their cry, His rebuke of wind and sea, and their wonder disclose both little faith and lordship over creation.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Matthew 8:23–27.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The ship was covered - So man's extremity is God's opportunity. Why are ye fearful - Then he rebuked the winds - First, he composed their spirits, and then the sea.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 8:23–27)

reformed.quote: And when he had entered into a ship Mark says that other little ships crossed along with him: but that Christ entered into his own ship with his disciples Luke too quotes his words: Matthew is more concise. They agree, however, as to the leading fact, that Christ laid himself down to rest, and that, while he was asleep, a tempest suddenly arose.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 8:23–27)

verses.text: When he got into a boat, his disciples followed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Disciples follow into the boat—obedience that will soon be tested by water and wind. Following is true before the crisis arrives.

Grace has brought them this far; they still must keep trusting when the lake turns violent.
verses.reformedNotes:
Embarking fulfills the earlier order. Disciples follow the King into danger He already knows.

The storm ahead is not outside His plan. Their following places them under the same providence that rules wind and wave.

verses.text: Behold, a violent storm came up on the sea, so much that the boat was covered with the waves; but he was asleep.
verses.arminianNotes:
Great storm, swamped boat, sleeping Lord—the contrast is pastoral and piercing. Crisis can feel like divine absence even when Jesus is present.

Classical Arminians allow deep fear in believers. Faith is summoned to cry out rather than despair; His sleep is not indifference.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Behold” marks the shock. Nature rages; the Creator naps. The scene is designed to reveal hearts and glory.

Sleep is not neglect but sovereign calm. The Lord who appoints the storm also rests in the boat—fear meets providence.

verses.text: The disciples came to him and woke him up, saying, “Save us, Lord! We are dying!”
verses.arminianNotes:
They wake Him with a true prayer: Save us, Lord. Panic and faith tangle—“We are dying” beside “Lord.”

Imperfect faith may still cry rightly. Grace invites the plea; responsibility is to bring fear to Jesus rather than only to the oars.
verses.reformedNotes:
The cry is half right: Lord, save. Perishing language shows little faith’s math—present waves outweigh present Christ.

Even weak prayer reaches Him. He will answer, then diagnose. Salvation in the storm comes from the One they woke.

verses.text: He said to them, “Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?” Then he got up, rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm.
verses.arminianNotes:
Little faith is named, then winds and sea are rebuked into great calm. Jesus addresses fear before He addresses weather—discipleship of the heart.

The passage carries a call to grow. Assisting grace strengthens trust; believers are responsible not to let fear contradict the Lord in the boat.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus asks his question first and works the miracle second. Little faith is true in the elect yet rebuked. Then creation obeys its Lord—great calm.

The same voice that justifies and sanctifies stills storms. Fear shrinks when sovereignty is seen; calm is His gift and His credential.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm little faith rebuked and Christ as Lord of nature. Arminians emphasize growth in trust under assisting grace; Calvinists typically underline God’s sovereign calm—fear yields as the disciples glimpse who sleeps in their boat.

verses.text: The men marveled, saying, “What kind of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Marvel asks the right question: What sort of man? Creation’s obedience points beyond a mere teacher to divine authority.

Keep following the question to its answer. Grace keeps revealing Jesus; faith responds by deeper worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Wonder is incomplete confession moving toward truth. Winds and sea obey—Psalm-like dominion in a man.

This is the Lord of Hosts in flesh. The storm narrative catechizes Christology; providence has preached His deity to trembling disciples.
